title: The Letter Lincoln Never Sent
text:
In early July 1863 the Union army under General George Meade beat Robert E. Lee at Gettysburg. Lee retreated south, but heavy rains swelled the Potomac River and trapped his battered army on the Maryland side. In Washington, Abraham Lincoln waited for Meade to strike the final blow. Meade hesitated, held councils of war, and on the night of July 13 Lee slipped across the river.

Lincoln was bitterly disappointed. On July 14 he sat down and wrote Meade a letter. He told the general that he did not believe Meade appreciated "the magnitude of the misfortune involved in Lee's escape," that the war could have been ended, and that he was distressed beyond measure by it.

Then Lincoln put the letter away. It was found among his papers, with an endorsement in his hand noting it was never sent or signed. Meade, who had already offered to resign after hearing of the President's displeasure, stayed in command of the Army of the Potomac until the end of the war. Lincoln had written out his anger in full, and in the end kept the general he still needed.
lesson: When you are furious, write the letter if it helps, then wait before sending it. Ask whether it will fix anything or only cost you someone you still need.
source: Abraham Lincoln, letter to George G. Meade, July 14, 1863 (unsent), Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, ed. Roy P. Basler, vol. 6
